Content:
Good news is that we can extend the Gram-Schmidt process. Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

Step 3. Next, let [MATH: S=\textrm{Span}(\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2).] We find [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3}] using the formula

Content:
[MATH: v_{3}|= a_{3}− proj_{S}a_{3}; = a_{3}− proj_{v_{1}}a_{3} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{3}; = a_{3} − (a_{3} ⋅ v_{1})/(v_{1} ⋅ v_{1})v_{1} − (a_{3} ⋅ v_{2})/(v_{2} ⋅ v_{2})v_{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

Step 1: We set [MATH: [1; 1; 1; 1]]

Step 2: We set [MATH: [1; 1; − 1; − 1]]

Step 3. Next, we find [MATH: \mathbf{v}_3] using the formula

[MATH: v_{3}|= a_{3} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{3} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{3}; = a_{3} − (a_{3} ⋅ v_{1})/(v_{1} ⋅ v_{1})v_{1} − (a_{3} ⋅ v_{2})/(v_{2} ⋅ v_{2})v_{2}.]

Applying the formula for [MATH: \mathbf{v}_3] in our case gives

[MATH: v_{3}|= [− 1; 0; − 2; 1] − (− (2)/(4))[1; 1; 1; 1] − (0)/(4)[1; 1; − 1; − 1]; = [− 1; 0; − 2; 1] + (1)/(2)[1; 1; 1; 1] − 0[1; 1; − 1; − 1]; = (1)/(2)(2[− 1; 0; − 2; 1] + [1; 1; 1; 1]); = [− (1)/(2); (1)/(2); − (3)/(2); (3)/(2)].]

Finally, [MATH: a=-\dfrac 1 2,] [MATH: c=-\dfrac 3 2,] and [MATH: \dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}{\left(-\dfrac 1 2\right)} = 3.]

But what do we do if the original basis we are given doesn't contain any orthogonal vectors? Well, then we make them orthogonal using the Gram-Schmidt process!

Content:
Given a basis [MATH: \,\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{a}_n\}] for a non zero subspace [MATH: V], we can get an orthogonal basis for [MATH: V] by defining the vectors
[MATH: v_{1}|= a_{1}; v_{2}|= a_{2} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{2}; v_{3}|= a_{3} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{3} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{3}; ⋮|= ⋮; v_{n}|= a_{n} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{n} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{n} − ⋯ − proj_{v_{n − 1}}a_{n}.]

Content:
The set of vectors [MATH: \{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\}] will be an orthogonal basis for [MATH: V].

Content:
Here, we build up the orthogonal basis one vector at a time, by taking away from each basis vector its orthogonal projection onto each of the [MATH: 1]-dimensional subspaces spanned by one of the orthogonal basis vectors found already.

Content:
Furthermore, if we want to find an orthonormal basis, we just have to normalize the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_i] for [MATH: i=1,2,\dots,n.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Gram-Schmidt Process

Content:
But what do we do if the original basis we are given doesn't contain any orthogonal vectors? Well, then we make them orthogonal using the Gram-Schmidt process!

Content:
Given a basis [MATH: \,\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{a}_n\}] for a non zero subspace [MATH: V], we can get an orthogonal basis for [MATH: V] by defining the vectors
[MATH: v_{1}|= a_{1}; v_{2}|= a_{2} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{2}; v_{3}|= a_{3} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{3} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{3}; ⋮|= ⋮; v_{n}|= a_{n} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{n} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{n} − ⋯ − proj_{v_{n − 1}}a_{n}.]

Content:
The set of vectors [MATH: \{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\}] will be an orthogonal basis for [MATH: V].

Content:
Here, we build up the orthogonal basis one vector at a time, by taking away from each basis vector its orthogonal projection onto each of the [MATH: 1]-dimensional subspaces spanned by one of the orthogonal basis vectors found already.

Content:
Furthermore, if we want to find an orthonormal basis, we just have to normalize the vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_i] for [MATH: i=1,2,\dots,n.]

EXPLANATION

Step 2. We find the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] orthogonal to [MATH: \text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}] using the usual formula:

[MATH: v_{2}|= a_{2} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{2}; = a_{2} − (a_{2} ⋅ v_{1})/(v_{1} ⋅ v_{1})v_{1}; = [1; 2; 2] − (3)/(3)[− 1; 1; 1]; = [2; 1; 1].]

Step 3. We find the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_3] orthogonal to [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \}] using the usual formula:

[MATH: v_{3}|= a_{3} − proj_{v_{1}}a_{3} − proj_{v_{2}}a_{3}; = a_{3} − (a_{3} ⋅ v_{1})/(v_{1} ⋅ v_{1})v_{1} − (a_{3} ⋅ v_{2})/(v_{2} ⋅ v_{2})v_{2}; = [2; 1; − 2] − (− (3)/(3))[− 1; 1; 1] − (3)/(6)[2; 1; 1]; = [2; 1; − 2] + [− 1; 1; 1] − (1)/(2)[2; 1; 1]; = (1)/(2)(2[2; 1; − 2] + 2[− 1; 1; 1] − [2; 1; 1]); = [0; (3)/(2); − (3)/(2)].]

Finally, [MATH: b=\dfrac 3 2,] [MATH: c=-\dfrac 3 2,] and [MATH: \dfrac{b}{c} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac 3 2\right)}{\left(-\dfrac 3 2\right)}=-1.]
